topics: Prefix vs KV cache use cases
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-24 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Diaz (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Horizon - Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Platform), Sofia Reyes (Security), Tom (PM)

[00:00] Ava: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i think we've got about 50 minutes, we want to run through the Optimize walkthrough today focusing on batching and caching recommendations, and a cost model, ok?
[00:08] Maya: yep sounds good, we'll be listening for latency tradeoffs — our SLAs are 200ms p95 for single-turn responses for our fraud-check assistant.
[00:15] Carlos: great, quick agenda — we'll cover batching basics, prefix vs KV cache, show some numbers from our cost model, and then go to specific config suggestions for Horizon's workload.
[00:24] Tom: quick context, we run on EKS in us-east-1, 2 g4dn clusters for inference today, and traffic peaks at about 80 rps, but we expect bursts up to 300 rps during batch windows.
[00:36] Liam: also note we have strict PCI-adjacent requirements and we need KMS integration for keys.
[00:42] Carlos: understood, we'll call out private deployment and KMS options.

[02:10] Carlos: ok batching — the tradeoff is simple: bigger batches = better GPU utilization and lower per-token cost but higher tail latency. so we recommend dynamic batching with a small latency budget, e.g. target 50ms batching window for low-latency requests, and separate high-throughput queues for asynchronous work.
[02:34] Maya: can you quantify savings? like percent cost down for 1M tokens?
[02:38] Carlos: yeah rough ballpark from our model — with dynamic batching and prefix/KV cache we typically see 30-60% reduction in per-token cost depending on prompt re-use and average prompt length. for Horizon's profile (short prompts, high repeat prefixes) i'm estimating ~45% savings.
[02:52] Ava: to add, the model choice matters too — smaller quantized variants for low-risk routes reduce cost. we can show a table after.

[05:15] [screen share starts] Carlos: here is the benchmark spreadsheet — columns: model, instance type, qps, batch size, avg latency p50/p95, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens.
[05:29] [05:33] Carlos: for example, 8x A10 + llama-2-13b-quant yields X tokens/sec, but 4x A100 with kv-caching tuned gives lower cost for chat style flows. (note: some transcription shows model names slightly off, e.g., "llama2-13b-quant" -> sometimes transcribed as "lama two")

[07:00] Maya: tell me more about prefix vs kv cache - when to use each?
[07:06] Carlos: good q — prefix cache good when you have repeated initial context, like user profile + product description, you cache pre-computed KV states for first N tokens so you don't re-run attention for that prefix. KV cache is better for long-running sessions where the kv cache grows, or for re-using recent tokens across similar queries. in practice we often use both: prefix for static repeated context, kv for recent conversational state.
[07:35] Liam: does KV cache require sticky routing to the same GPU?
[07:40] Carlos: yes sticky routing or session affinity for warm KV cache is typical; we support automatic session routing and fallback to cold start if instance unavailable. we also have a fallback policy that routes to a compatible smaller model if capacity constrained.

[10:22] Ava: operational notes — prefix caching reduces compute per request but increases memory usage on the host for stored KV. you can control retention and eviction policies. trade-offs depend on average prompt length and reuse ratio.

[12:45] Carlos: now the cost model — here's a simplified example using Horizon numbers: assume 1M requests/month, avg 120 tokens per request, 80% prefix reuse, dynamic batching target 50ms, we project hosted per-token cost = $0.018/token (baseline), with batching+prefix+kv we can get equivalent down to $0.0098/token, roughly 45% savings, and with Dedicated reserved GPU pools that can drop cost further but requires commitment.
[13:20] Maya: can you show sensitivity if reuse is only 30%?
[13:25] Carlos: sure, reuse at 30% pushes savings to ~20-25% because caching benefits diminish; that's in the sheet.

[17:10] [minor crosstalk] Sofia: on security, we need SOC2 evidence, audit logs for token-level access, and deterministic encryption with KMS; also data residency — can Redwood guarantee logs stay in our VPC or private deployment?
[17:25] Ava: yes — for Horizon we'd recommend Private deployment (VPC) or Dedicated with VPC peering; logs and telemetry can be sent to your S3 and we support customer-managed KMS/HSM for key rotation. we'll send the SOC 2 and design docs.
[17:40] Sofia: also need RBAC and SSO -> SAML.
[17:45] Ava: supported, we'll attach SSO config docs.

[22:00] Carlos: demo snippet — configuring batching in the Console: set dynamic window to 50ms, max batch size 64, split routes by latency sensitive vs batchable. set prefix cache TTL to 24 hours and include retention policy for non-PII keys.
[22:28] Carlos: show JSON snippet: {"route":"fraud-check","batching":{"mode":"dynamic","window_ms":50,"max_batch_size":64},"cache":{"prefix_ttl":"24h","kv_enabled":true,"sticky_sessions":true}}  (transcription may mangle braces)

[26:05] Tom: any gotchas for our existing EKS setup? we want minimal infra changes.
[26:12] Carlos: not many; if you use Redwood Hosted API you only need to route requests. if you want Private we provide a control plane and a small on-prem agent for model serving. Dedicated requires setting up reserved pools and autoscaling policies but we can help. KV cache in Private mode stores cache in local GPU memory; for multi-node you need sticky routing.

[30:50] Ava: question on rollback and safety — can we A/B a new config?
[30:55] Carlos: yes Console supports canary rollouts and automatic fallback to cold model on errors; you can define metric-based rollbacks (latency, error rate).

[34:30] Maya: what about quantization steps? we can't accept big accuracy regressions on some prompts used for compliance checks.
[34:38] Carlos: we recommend per-route quality monitoring and eval sets; start with int8 quant for non-critical routes, keep critical flows on fp16 or higher accuracy variants. Redwood Optimize will surface regression alerts when eval sets deviate.

[37:12] [screen share - cost breakdown] Carlos: here's example per-route ledger: tokens, compute cost, infra charge, caching savings, total effective $/1M tokens. we project for Horizon: Baseline hosted = $18k / 1M tokens (placeholder), optimized = $9.8k / 1M tokens. again depends on reuse and batch windows.

[41:00] Liam: curious about burst handling — during peak 300 rps will batching add latency spikes?
[41:08] Carlos: dynamic batching respects latency SLO by setting time window and queue depth; for hard real-time we route to a low-latency dedicated pool. you can provision burst capacity and set automatic fallback so user-facing requests don't see tail spikes.

[44:20] Ava: ok to recap quick?
[44:24] Maya: yes please.
[44:25] Ava: recap — recommendations: 1) Pilot hosted/Dedicated hybrid: route latency-sensitive routes to low-latency pool, batchable routes to high-throughput pool with dynamic batching target 50ms. 2) Implement prefix cache for repeated context (TTL 24h) and KV cache for session reuse with sticky routing. 3) Use quantized smaller variants for non-critical flows, keep critical on high-accuracy models. 4) We'll run a 1-week pilot benchmark and share expected savings in spreadsheet. 5) Redwood to send SOC2/KMS/SSO docs for security review.
[45:05] Tom: sounds good, we'll need pricing and pilot plan.
[45:12] Ava: action items — we'll send pricing and schedule kickoff.

[50:00] [wrap up] Maya: thanks, that was useful; Carlos, we'll share the sample traffic and prompt set; Sofia will follow up on compliance list.
[50:12] Ava: great, thanks all, we'll follow up via email with the items discussed.

End of transcript. Note: transcription contains minor errors and mis-typed model names; speaker labels approximate.
